'''''Commelina benghalensis''''', commonly known as the '''Benghal dayflower''', '''tropical spiderwort''', or '''wandering Jew''',<ref>Umberto Quattrocchi. ''CRC World Dictionary of Plant Names: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms. Synonyms, and Etymology.'' CRC Press, 1999. p.594. {{ISBN|9780849326738}}</ref> ''kanshira'' in [[Bengali language|Bengali]], is a perennial herb native to tropical Asia and Africa. It has been widely introduced to areas outside its native range, including to the [[neotropics]], Hawaii, the [[West Indies]] and to both coasts of North America. It has a long flowering period, from spring to fall in subtropical areas, and throughout the year closer to the equator.<ref name="Kaul et al 2002">{{cite journal | last1 = Kaul | first1 = Veenu | last2 = Sharma | first2 = Namrata |  last3 = Koul | first3 = A. K. | title = Reproductive effort and sex allocation strategy in Commelina benghalensis L., a common monsoon weed | journal = Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society | volume = 140 | pages = 403–413 | date = June 2002 | issue = 4 | language = en | doi=10.1046/j.1095-8339.2002.00082.x| doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Santhosh Nampy et al 2013">{{cite journal | last1 = Santhosh Nampy | last2 = Sheba M. Joseph | last3 = Manudev | first3 = K. M. | title = The genus Commelina (Commelinaceae) in Andaman & Nicobar Islands, India with one new species and three new records | journal = Phytotaxa | volume = 87 | issue = 2 | pages = 19–29 | publisher = Magnolia Press | date = 19 February 2013 | language = en | doi = 10.11646/phytotaxa.87.2.1 | bibcode = 2013Phytx..87...19N }}</ref> It is often associated with disturbed soils.

In both it native range and areas where it has been introduced it is usually considered a weed, sometimes a serious one. In the United States it has been placed on the [[Federal Noxious Weed List]]. It is considered a moderate weed of rice cultivation in Asia.<ref>{{Citation|title=A practical field guide to weeds of rice in Asia |author=Caton, B. P. |author2=M. Mortimer |author3=J. E. Hill |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ver3qCQF9EEC&q=field+guide |year=2004 |pages=22–23 |publisher=International Rice Research Institute|isbn=978-971-22-0191-2 }}</ref> In its native range of sub-Saharan Africa, India, Sri Lanka, and much of Southeast Asia, it is considered a serious weed of an enormous range of crops from tea and coffee to cassava and peanuts. Additional agricultural damage is caused by the fact that it can host the [[nematode]] ''[[Meloidogyne incognita]]'' and the [[Groundnut rosette virus]].<ref name=Holm>{{citation|last=Holm|first=Leroy G.|title=The World's Worst Weeds|pages=[https://archive.org/details/worldweedsnatura0000unse/page/225 225–235]|isbn=978-0-471-04701-8|publisher=University Press of Hawaii|place=Honolulu|year=1977|url=https://archive.org/details/worldweedsnatura0000unse/page/225}}</ref>

In China it is used as a medicinal herb that is said to have diuretic, [[febrifuge|febrifugal]] and anti-inflammatory effects, while in [[Pakistan]] it is used to cure swellings of the skin, [[leprosy]] and as a laxative.

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Commelina benghalensis W IMG 1553.jpg|thumb|190px|left|''Commelina benghalensis'' in [[Hyderabad, India]]. ]]
[[File:Commelina benghalensis (Benghal dayflower) in Kolkata.jpg|thumb|Commelina benghalensis (Benghal dayflower) in Kolkata, West Bengal, India]]
''Commelina benghalensis''  is a wide-ranging plant, being native to tropical and subtropical Asia and Africa, an area otherwise known as the [[paleotropics]]. In China it is commonly associated with wet locations. There it can be found from near sea level up to 2300 metres. It is present from the [[Province (China)|provinces]] of [[Hebei]] and [[Shandong]] in the northeast, west to [[Sichuan]] and in all provinces south to [[Hainan]], the southernmost province. It is also found in [[Taiwan]].<ref name=chinaflora>{{Citation| last =Hong| first =Deyuan; DeFillipps, Robert A.| contribution =Commelina diffusa | year =2000| title =Flora of China| editor-last =Wu| editor-first =Z. Y. |editor2=Raven, P.H. |editor3=Hong, D.Y.| volume =24| pages =36| place=Beijing| publisher =Science Press; St. Louis: Missouri Botanical Garden Press| contribution-url =http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=222000040| access-date =21 June 2007}}</ref> In Japan the plant is restricted to the southern portions of the country from the southern [[Kantō region]] westward and including the islands of [[Shikoku]] and [[Kyūshū]].<ref>{{citation| title=Flora of Japan (in English)| last=Ohwi| first=Jisaburo| year=1965| publisher=Smithsonian Institution| location=Washington, D.C.| page=271}}</ref> Although its roots and tubers are used as a food source, ''C. benghalensis'' is not cultivated in [[Ethiopia]], where it grows as a weed.<ref>Zemede Asfaw, [http://www.bioversityinternational.org/publications/Web_version/500/ch08.htm "Conservation and use of traditional vegetables in Ethiopia"] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120707210646/http://www.bioversityinternational.org/publications/Web_version/500/ch08.htm |date=7 July 2012 }}, ''Proceedings of the IPGRI International Workshop on Genetic Resources of Traditional Vegetables in Africa'' (Nairobi, 29–31 August 1995)</ref>

The plant has also been widely introduced beyond its range to the [[neotropics]]<ref name=flora/> - the southeastern United States, California, Hawaii, [[Cuba]], [[Jamaica]], [[Puerto Rico]], Martinique, [[Montserrat]], [[Barbados]] and [[Saint Vincent and the Grenadines|St Vincent]]. In Puerto Rico the plant is known from a single collection from [[Cayey]].<ref name=Puerto>{{citation| last=Acevedo-Rodriguez| first=Pedro |author2=Strong, Mark T.| journal=Contributions of the United States National Herbarium| title=Monocotyledons and Gymnosperms of Puerto Rico and Virgin Islands| volume=52| pages=158| year=2005}}</ref> In the southeastern United States the plant was collected in 1928, while it was first collected in Hawaii in 1909.<ref name=rare/> In the southeastern states it is present in Florida, [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], [[Louisiana]]<ref name=flora>{{Citation| last =Faden| first =Robert | contribution =Commelina benghalensis| year =2006| title =Flora of North America online| editor=Flora of North America Editorial Committee | volume =22| contribution-url =http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=222000036| place=New York & Oxford| publisher =Oxford University Press| access-date =12 December 2007}}</ref> and [[North Carolina]] and spreading.<ref name=weed>{{Citation| last1= Webster| first1= Theodore M.| journal=Weed Technology| volume=19| issue=3| pages=501–508| title=Tropical Spiderwort (Commelina benghalensis): A Tropical Invader Threatens Agroecosystems of the Southern United States| year=2005| doi= 10.1614/WT-04-234R.1| last2= Burton| first2= Michael G.| last3= Culpepper| first3= A. Stanley| last4= York| first4= Alan C.| last5= Prostko| first5= Eric P.| bibcode= 2005WeedT..19..501W| s2cid= 85779088}}</ref> It was added to the [[Federal Noxious Weed List]] in 1983,<ref name=rare>{{citation| last=Faden| first=Robert B.| journal=Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden| volume=80| pages=208–218| title=The misconstrued and rare species of Commelina (Commelinaceae) in the eastern United States| year=1993| issue=1| doi=10.2307/2399824| jstor=2399824| publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden Press| bibcode=1993AnMBG..80..208F}}</ref> and by 2003 was considered the most serious pest of Georgia's cotton crop due to widely used herbicides such as [[glyphosate]] having little effect on it.<ref name=weed/> It was introduced separately to California in the 1980s, making it the only introduced species of ''Commelina'' in the western United States.<ref name=flora/><ref name=rare/> It is associated with disturbed soils such as yards, lawns and cultivated areas, especially in cotton crops and orange groves.<ref name=rare/><ref name=weed/>

==Morphology==
In Jammu, India, this plant is an annual, growing from May to December and flowering from June to October.<ref name="Kaul et al 2002"/> In the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, located closer to the equator, it is a perennial, flowering around the year.<ref name="Santhosh Nampy et al 2013"/>

''Commelina benghalensis'' produces three types of branches - aerial or negatively geotropic ones, subaerial or diageotropic ones, and underground or positively geotropic ones. The underground branches do not bear leaves.<ref name="Kaul et al 2002"/>

==Reproduction==
Bengal dayflowers display an enormous diversity in reproductive systems. It produces three types of flowers -male ([[chasmogamous]]), [[hermaphrodite]] chasmogamous and hermaphrodite [[cleistogamous]]. All three types develop on aerial branches, but only hermaphrodite chasmogamous flowers develop on subaerial branches, and only cleistogamous flowers develop on underground branches. Finally, some plants may produce female flowers on aerial branches. Developing flowers are covered in mucilaginous spathes.<ref name="Kaul et al 2002"/>

Flowers are [[zygomorphic]]. The petals are blue. The androecium (male organ) has six [[stamen]]s, of which only three are fertile. One of the fertile stamens is longer and yellow; the other two are shorter and grey in colour. Pollen grains are yellowish coloured and capsule shaped.
[[File:Pollen grains of Commelina benghalensis.jpg|thumb|Pollen grains of Commelina benghalensis]]
The gynoecium (female organ) has three joined [[carpel]]s. Aerial and subaerial branch flowers have five ovules per ovary; underground branch flowers have three.<ref name="Kaul et al 2002"/>

Seeds are ovoid; 2 mm long and 1.5 mm wide.{{citation needed|date=December 2019}} There are four types of seeds - large and small aerial and underground. Plants from large underground seeds grow fastest in the first 2–4 weeks and so seem to have better competitive ability. All the other types of seeds have a dormancy period. They may be produced to survive stressful periods (e.g. droughts) or to spread to new areas. Kim Sang Yeol found that most (75-77%) seeds were of the small aerial type, and that only 2-4% of seeds were underground seeds.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Kim | first = Sang Yeol | title = Growth and development of ''Commelina benghalensis'' L. from four seed types | journal = Korean Journal of Weed Science | volume = 18 | issue = 1 | pages = 42–47 | date = 1998 | doi = 10.3346/jkms.2003.18.1.42 | pmid = 12589085 | pmc = 3055002 | language = en, ko}}</ref>

==Uses==
In China, the plant is used medicinally as a diuretic, [[febrifuge]] and anti-inflammatory.<ref name=chinaflora/> In [[Pakistan]] it is used as animal [[fodder]] and also eaten by humans as a vegetable. It is also used there medicinally, but with different purported effects, including as a laxative and to cure inflammations of the skin as well as [[leprosy]].<ref name=Pakistan>{{Citation| last =Qaiser| first=M. |author2=Jafri, S.M.H.| contribution =Commelina benghalensis| year =1975| title =Flora of Pakistan| editor-last =Ali| editor-first =S.I. |editor2=Qaiser, M.| volume =84| pages =10| contribution-url =http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=222000036| place=St. Louis| publisher =University of Karachi & Missouri Botanical Garden}}</ref> The people of [[Nepal]] eat the young leaves as a vegetable, use a paste derived from the plant to treat burns, and treat indigestion with a juice produced from the roots.<ref>{{citation|last=Manandhar|first=N. P. |author2=Manandhar, Sanjay| title=Plants and People of Nepal| page=167| isbn=0-88192-527-6| publisher=Timber Press| year=2002}}</ref> Its use as a [[famine food]] in India has been recorded. In southeast Asia and Africa it is used as fodder and also medicinally as a [[poultice]].<ref name=Holm/>
